transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-04
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Ravi (Cascade CTO), Sofia (Head of Platform), Ethan (SRE), Anika (Security)

Summary:
High-level discovery on uptime/continuity requirements for Cascade's planned LLM features (personalization, content tagging). Focus on service continuity, multi-region routing, fallback policies between Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments, SLA expectations, and security constraints (KMS, audit logs, SSO).

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Failure modes and RTO/RPO expectations
- Routing and fallback strategies (region, model variants, capacity tiers)
- Security/compliance gating for private deployment
- Pilot and next steps

Action items (recorded during call): see metadata section

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining second half of today, is this still a good time?
[00:12] Ravi (Cascade): yep, good to go. sorry for the slight delay we had another sync earlier.
[00:16] Sofia (Cascade): hi all, excited to dig in. we wanted to figure out how you think about keeping chat and tagging features live during outages.
[00:22] Liam (Redwood SE): great. quick intro — I’m Liam from Redwood infra team, I’ll cover routing and fallback patterns. Maya will handle commercial/next steps.
[00:30] Ethan (Cascade SRE): quick note — our main goal is to keep P95 under 400ms for the personalization route; users notice anything higher. we have around 120 req/s at peak per region.
[00:40] Jordan (Redwood): thanks, that helps. and what percent of traffic is read-only embeddings vs chat gen?
[00:47] Ravi: roughly 60% embeddings (batchy), 40% generation, but gen is the latency-sensitive one.
[00:54] Maya: perfect. can you tell us about your current infra — are you cloud-only, multi-region?
[01:02] Sofia: we run primary in us-west-2, secondary in eu-west-1 for users in EMEA. most services are cloud-managed, but security wants a path to private deployment for sensitive content.
[01:12] Anika (Security): yeah, from compliance we need customer-managed keys, audit logs, and SSO integration — ideally SAML/Okta.
[01:20] Liam: ok. that aligns with our Private offering. Quick caveat, when people say private they mean different things — do you expect on-prem air-gapped or VPC with customer KMS?
[01:30] Anika: VPC with KMS is our preference. on-prem is a later conversation.
[01:36] Liam: got it. so VPC private deployment is feasible — we provide a private control plane and you can bring your KMS/HSM. audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM.
[01:45] Ravi: good. can we drill into failure scenarios? for example if us-west has a GPU pool outage what does Redwood do?
[01:53] Jordan: there are a few levers — multi-region routing, model fallbacks (smaller quantized models), and capacity-tier fallbacks (dedicated -> hosted -> best-effort). we can route traffic to eu-west or to a lower-cost model variant automatically.
[02:07] Ethan: automatic routing is great but we care about correctness. if we route to a different model variant are there semantic differences we should measure?
[02:15] Liam: yes you'll see differences. part of pilot work is to capture evals across variants so we can set quality thresholds and only failover if quality delta is acceptable.
[02:24] Ravi: what about latency? routing to eu-west will add RTT, that could break our P95 target.
[02:30] Jordan: absolutely — prefer local fallbacks like smaller quantized models in same region first. cross-region is last resort for availability. you can set policy priorities: prefer same-region quantized, then cross-region, then degraded response (e.g., cached answer or 503).
[02:44] Sofia: can Redwood do graceful degradation — say return cached responses for non-critical routes and blocking for critical ones?
[02:51] Liam: yes, route-level policies are supported. you can mark routes critical and pin them to Dedicated capacity. non-critical routes can be directed to hosted or serve stale/cached.
[03:00] Anika: auditability is key. during a failover we need logs showing which model and region served the request for forensic purposes.
[03:08] Jordan: we attach request-level metadata (model_id, region, fallover_reason) to audit logs. those logs can be forwarded to your cloud logging or SIEM.
[03:18] Ravi: ok, realistic numbers — what SLAs do you offer for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?
[03:24] Maya: Hosted has best-effort availability with published latency profiles; Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs; Private can have contract-level SLAs depending on deployment details. we can share the SLA doc.
[03:36] Ethan: what does SLA mean for mitigation during overload — do you do automatic throttling or queueing?
[03:42] Liam: we support burst buffers and graceful shedding. you can set per-route rate limits and token budgets. we also support auto-scaling on Dedicated pools and surge capacity from hosted as fallback if configured.
[03:55] Sofia: what's the failure window for automatic failover? how fast can traffic be rerouted?
[04:02] Jordan: typically failover to another pool or region is within tens of seconds if health checks detect an issue; model-variant substitution can be near-instant once the variant is warmed or KV cache is present. cold starts for a large model might be minutes.
[04:16] Ravi: tens of seconds might be a lot for user-facing features. any strategies to reduce that?
[04:21] Liam: keep a warmed warm-standby pool (lower-sized GPU) or maintain a hot quantized variant with hot KV cache. that's the usual approach to hit sub-5s recovery for gen routes.
[04:32] Ethan: how do you manage KV cache across regions? consistency is difficult.
[04:37] Jordan: KV cache is per-inference node; for cross-region failover you either accept cold cache or proactively replicate prefixes for critical sessions. it's a tradeoff — replication costs tokens/throughput.
[04:50] Anika: security question — KMS integration, do you store any customer keys?
[04:55] Maya: no, for Private with customer-managed KMS we don't hold your keys. for Hosted we offer envelope encryption and optional customer-supplied keys depending on plan.
[05:04] Sofia: and audit logs retention — we need 1 year of immutable logs for compliance, can you support?
[05:10] Jordan: yes, we can forward to your blob store or SIEM and support retention policies; for Private you control retention.
[05:17] Ravi: network topology — if we run VPC Private, do you require peering or a VPN?
[05:23] Liam: we support multiple connectivity patterns: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, or VPN for on-prem. depends on firewall rules and you can restrict egress.
[05:31] Sophie (sic) [note: mis-transcript of Sofia]: is there any PCI/privacy or data residency enforcement built in?
[05:37] Maya: you can pin model deployments to region and restrict data residency; for extra controls we support on-prem deployments.
[05:44] Ethan: commercial question — if we want Dedicated reserved capacity what typical lead times and commitment sizes?
[05:50] Maya: reserved Dedicated usually has 2–6 week lead time for capacity provisioning depending on region and model; minimum commitments depend on GPU class — we can share a sizing guide.
[05:59] Ravi: cost tradeoffs are important — we might accept slightly higher latency for big cost reductions. can we set a cost-first policy?
[06:06] Jordan: yes policies support cost vs latency weighting. you can define a cost budget and we'll prefer cheaper model variants or delayed batching to fit under budget while attempting to meet latency SLOs.
[06:16] Maya: quick question for procurement side — any legal or audit checks we should expect early?
[06:23] Anika: we'll need SOC2 type 2, proof of encryption at rest, KMS integration, and a data processing addendum. also access controls — RBAC and SSO.
[06:33] Liam: we can share redwood compliance pack and SAML docs.
[06:36] Sofia: can we run a short resiliency POC — like induce a failed pool and observe failover?
[06:41] Jordan: definitely, we do resilience drills with customers. typical POC: mirror traffic to Redwood test endpoints, simulate node failure, verify failover and quality metrics.
[06:52] Ethan: what's your observability surface during POC? we need per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns.
[06:59] Liam: Redwood Console offers per-route dashboards, token cost, tracing hooks, and raw log exports. we can give you a demo account for the POC.
[07:08] Ravi: and devotion to privacy — can we scrub telemetry or route logs to our SIEM without PII?
[07:15] Maya: yes, we support configurable scrubbing and can redact PII before logs leave our control plane.
[07:21] Anika: one more — who owns the rollback plan if a new model rollout causes regressions?
[07:27] Jordan: rollouts are controlled via canary/A-B and automatic fallback policies; you can set auto-rollback on quality regression thresholds.
[07:35] Sofia: if we do cross-region failover for a subset of traffic, can we split by user segments?
[07:42] Liam: yes routing rules can be per-tenant, per-route, or header-based.
[07:47] Ravi: timeline — we're aiming to begin a pilot in Q4 and have production readiness by Q1. does that seem realistic?
[07:55] Maya: yes that's reasonable. pilot in Q4 to validate latency and failover, then Dedicated or Private procurement by Q1 depending on results.
[08:03] Jordan: for pilot scope — recommend 2 critical routes (gen + tagging), 1 non-critical embeddings route, and resilience test plan.
[08:12] Ethan: ok fine. what's the primary risk you see from Redwood's side?
[08:17] Liam: primary risks are cold-start times for large models during failover and possible quality delta across quantized variants — mitigations are warm-standby pools and pre-warming KV caches.
[08:29] Ravi: anything we should prepare on our side?
[08:31] Maya: share traffic profile, SSO/KMS contacts, and define the quality thresholds for failover. we will then propose a pilot topology and cost estimate.
[08:39] Sofia: can you include a runbook example for incident ops?
[08:43] Jordan: yes we'll include a sample playbook showing detection, routing decision tree, and rollback steps.
[08:49] Maya: sounds good. shall we recap next steps?
[08:53] Ravi: go ahead.
[08:55] Maya: Redwood will: 1) send SOC2 and KMS integration docs by 2026-09-07, 2) SEs (Liam/Jordan) will send pilot topology and cost estimate by 2026-09-09, 3) schedule a pilot planning meeting for week of 2026-09-14. Cascade will: 1) provide traffic profile and top routes by 2026-09-08, 2) confirm SAML/KMS contacts.
[09:19] Anika: noted. thanks.
[09:22] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and calendar invites.
[09:26] Ravi: thanks all.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
